title: Infra failover cheatpad: node rotation, GPU swap, and emergency capacity binder
content:
Purpose:
A compact working runbook for on-call and SRE engineers to triage and recover from infra incidents impacting inference capacity: node-level GPU failures, planned or emergency GPU replacement, cordon/drain decisions when capacity is tight, cluster recovery steps, and a quick emergency capacity add blueprint. This is an operational cheatpad (not policy).

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood Inference hosted and dedicated clusters running GPU-backed nodes for serving runtime.
- Assumes Kubernetes control plane healthy; if control plane is degraded, follow k8s control-plane escalation first.
- Nodes are labeled with gpu-type (e.g., nvidia-a100-80gb), rack, and zone. Autoscaler is enabled but regulated by reserved capacity pools.
- Model artifacts may be large; cold-starts can be expensive. We aim to avoid full cold starts where possible.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: which customer / deployment impacted? Check alert and run current_incident.sh (internal script) to collect node, pod, and routing state.
2) Check cluster capacity: kubectl get nodes -l gpu=true -o wide and k8s autoscaler dashboard.
3) Identify failed node(s): kubectl describe node <node> and check GPU health metrics (prometheus: node_gpu_errors, gpu_temperature).
4) Determine impact surface: Are serving pods crashing, OOM, or stuck on ImagePull? Are KV caches evicted?
5) Decide immediate mitigation: reroute traffic to fallback model / region, or add temporary capacity.

Fast mitigations (pick one based on severity):
- Soft-fallback: update routing policy to route new requests to a smaller model variant for best-effort continuity (Console -> Rollouts -> On-call fallback).
- Burst-capacity: Fire the emergency capacity runbook (see section below) to bring up pre-configured spot / reserved nodes tainted with emergency=true to avoid regular autoscaler grabs.
- Cordon/drain: If node is flapping but still reachable, cordon + drain to squash failure domain and let pods reschedule.

Safe cordon & drain pattern for GPU-heavy serving nodes:
1) Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node-name>
2) Drain carefully to avoid model artifact re-pulls at scale (we prefer pod-by-pod migration where possible):
   - Recommended command for graceful migration: kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=30m
   - If draining many nodes simultaneously, stagger by rack to preserve capacity for heavy models. Use --pod-selector to move low-priority routes first.
3) For long-lived model processes that use local NVMe for KV cache, check annotations: kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep model-cache-path. If local cache will be lost, prefer rolling to nodes with warmed caches or pre-warmed images.
4) If pods fail to start elsewhere due to GPU resource fragmentation, consider taint-based placement: remove taints on temporary nodes or spin up nodes matching the same gpu-type.

When to replace GPU hardware vs. reboot:
- Quick reboot if node_unhealthy is: driver crash, GPU stuck, or transient PCIe errors and node reachable. Reboot steps: 1) cordon 2) drain 3) ssh into BMC and reboot to rescue mode 4) check dmesg and nvidia-smi after boot.
- Replace hardware (RMA) if persistent ECC, multiple GPU hardware errors, or vendor diagnostic tool returns non-recoverable. Open hardware-support ticket and mark node as decommissioning in inventory.

GPU replacement handoff (field engineer / vendor steps):
1) Create a single incident thread and note node inventory id and rack position.
2) Ensure node is cordoned and drained. Annotate k8s node: kubectl annotate node <node> replacement-needed=true by=<oncall>
3) Power down via BMC only after engineer onsite is confirmed. Provide vendor scripts for GPU insertion torque and anti-static checks.
4) After replacement, power on and run vendor diagnostics and a local nvidia-smi stress test.
5) Reinstall drivers if driver version mismatch detected (see "driver reconciliation" below).
6) Mark node ready: run kubelet health checks, remove annotation, kubectl uncordon <node>. Monitor scheduler to confirm pods land and model KV caches warm successfully.

Driver reconciliation checklist (post-GPU swap / after reboot):
- Verify kernel + driver compatibility: uname -r; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version --format=csv
- If kernel modules missing, follow our AMI recovery steps: install matching nvidia-driver package, run update-initramfs, and reboot. Document driver package version in the node inventory.

Emergency capacity binder (fast path to add serving capacity):
Goal: bring up nodes that are predictable, labeled, pre-warmed, and isolated from normal autoscaler to avoid billing surprises.
Prerequisites (pre-baked):
- AMI/VM image with correct driver, kubelet config, and pre-pulled container images (in our image registry: registry.redwood/serve:prewarm).
- terraform or cloud-ops runbook with a one-click varset for emergency-pool size.
- Pre-configured taint and label: taint node: emergency=true:NoSchedule label: emergency=true gpu-type=<type>
- Model artifacts tarball on fast object-store and init script that preloads KV cache for top-10 customer models.

Emergency-scale steps (15-45 minutes typical):
1) Kick off cloud-ops job (internal: tools/scale-up-emergency.sh --pool=emergency-gpu --count=3 --gpu=nvidia-a100-80gb).
2) Verify instances reach RUNNING and join the cluster: kubectl get nodes -l emergency=true
3) Ensure taints present and default scheduler won't use them: kubectl describe node <node> | grep Taints
4) Trigger prewarm: Run prewarm job to pull containers and restore KV snapshots: kubectl apply -f prewarm-job-emergency.yaml --selector=gpu-type=<type>
5) Once warmed, remove taint for controlled admission or create a dedicated emergency low-priority queue in the router to slowly shift traffic.
6) Monitor p95 latency and error rates; keep an eye on cost dashboard and inform finance slack channel (#ops-billing).

Validation checklist after capacity add or node replace:
- Prometheus alerts: no alert for node_gpu_errors for 30m, pod_restart_count stable.
- Smoke tests: run smoke_inference_test.sh against newly scheduled pods (target <50ms median for small models).
- KV cache warm: check custom metric kv_cache_hit_rate > 60% after traffic reaches 30% of baseline.
- Load test: ramp at 10% increments for 30m and validate latency SLOs.

Rollbacks and fallbacks:
- If new nodes fail to stabilize, cordon them and scale down emergency-pool. Re-enable routing fallback to smaller models or alternate region.
- If driver mismatch causes degradation after replacement, drain and mark node for further investigation; revert to rolling-replace with previous AMI image.

Post-incident: what to capture in the review (for incident review doc):
- Timeline with operator actions and exact kubectl/bmc commands executed.
- Which models/customers were impacted and for how long (from routing logs).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (dumped dmesg, nvidia-smi logs, vendor diag).
- Cost impact of emergency pool (hours * instance-type * price).
- Action items: patch AMI, automate prewarm job, add driver version check to node-exporter.

Short troubleshooting cheats (common failure modes):
- Pods Pending with Insufficient GPUs: check nodeAllocatable (kubectl describe node) and GPU resource label mismatch. Possibly new nodes advertise different gpu-type label.
- Slow scheduling during drain of many nodes: check kube-scheduler logs and API throttling; use smaller drain windows.
- ImagePullBackOff at scale: pre-pull images or increase registry concurrency limits.
- KV cache cold-start spike: if unavoidable, use staged rollout with traffic-shifting and synthetic warm traffic first.

Contacts & escalation shortcuts:
- Oncall SRE primary: paged via PagerDuty (SRE rota).
- Infra lead (hardware/vendor): Marcus Lee (pager: mobile + vendor contacts).
- Cloud ops owner: Sofia Ramos.
- Console / routing owner: Ethan Jacobs.
- Hardware vendor support: vendor-support@hw.example.com, urgent phone: +1-800-555-1001

Notes & known caveats:
- Do NOT mass-drain nodes that are all in the same AZ or rack when load is high; it will trigger a cascade of cold model loads.
- Emergency nodes should always be tainted until prewarm completes to avoid immediate overload of registry and NVMe bandwidth.
- Keep one node as a staging sink for model artifacts to test driver/AMI mismatch before uncordoning fleet.

Appendix: useful commands
- Collect node diagnostics: tools/collect-node-diagnostics.sh <node> (internal wrapper that gathers nvidia-smi, system journal, dmesg, kubelet logs)
- Cordon: kubectl cordon <node>
- Graceful drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=30m
- Annotate for replacement: kubectl annotate node <node> replacement-needed=true
